definition: Dissemble means to hide your true feelings, motives, or intentions behind a false appearance.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dissemble. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dissemble should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Though the diplomat privately distrusted the visiting officials, she chose to dissemble, greeting them with warm smiles and easy conversation.
Someone who hedges merely avoids giving a straight answer, while someone who dissembles actively wears a false front.
To dissemble is to hide your true feelings, but to defraud is to use deception to actually cheat someone out of something.

To feign is to fake one specific thing - you feign surprise, illness, or delight, putting on a single false display, and the word wants an object. To dissemble is broader and quieter: hiding your real feelings or intentions behind a whole false front, often across an entire conversation.

To dissimulate is the closest twin: it also means hiding your true feelings behind a false appearance. Dissimulate stresses covering up what is really there, while dissemble is the more common word and covers both masking what is real and acting out what is false - the diplomat's whole warm performance.

To pretend is the plain, everyday word for acting as if something false were true, and children do it openly in games. To dissemble is deliberate adult concealment: hiding real motives behind a composed, believable front. Pretending can be innocent play; dissembling is calculated cover.

When her brother asked why she kept sneaking off to make phone calls, Priya dissembled, claiming she was checking homework answers with a classmate.
In reality, she was coordinating every detail of his surprise graduation party.
Priya hides her true purpose behind a false but believable explanation, which is precisely what it means to dissemble.
Dissemble is usually used without an object, as in 'he dissembled when asked about his plans.' Do not confuse it with disassemble, which means to take something apart piece by piece.

At a country estate sale, the dealer Marta Voss spotted a smoke-darkened panel she believed was a lost seventeenth-century portrait.
Everything now depended on her ability to dissemble.
For two hours she handled lesser lots with careful interest, asked the auctioneer detailed questions about a chipped vase, and let her eyes pass over the panel as if it were furniture.
Inside, she was rehearsing bids; outside, she wore the mild boredom of a woman killing an afternoon.
A rival later admitted he had watched her face the whole sale and read nothing in it -- which, he said, should have been the clue itself.
